questions.question: What is the primary difference between a process and a thread in modern operating systems?
options: Processes share the same address space while threads have separate memory
A thread cannot be scheduled independently by the operating system kernel
Processes have significantly lower context switching overhead than threads
Threads within a process share the same memory space and address range
questions.explanation: Threads within the same process share code, data, and OS resources such as open files, whereas processes run in distinct address spaces.

questions.question: Which HTTP response status code indicates that the client request cannot be completed because authentication credentials are required?
questions.explanation: HTTP 401 Unauthorized indicates that the request requires user authentication or that the provided credentials are invalid.

questions.question: In relational database transactions, what does the ACID property of Atomicity guarantee?
options: Transactions execute independently without interleaved race conditions
All operations within a transaction succeed completely or none take effect
Data remains strictly consistent across all distributed nodes at all times
Committed transactions survive subsequent server crashes or power failures
questions.explanation: Atomicity enforces an all-or-nothing rule: if any part of a transaction fails, the entire transaction is rolled back.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm degrades to O(n^2) worst-case time when the array is already sorted and the last element is always chosen as the pivot?
questions.explanation: Standard Quick Sort partitions poorly when an already sorted array is pivoted on an extreme boundary element, producing O(n^2) work.

questions.question: In the JavaScript and Node.js runtime, which mechanism allows asynchronous operations without freezing execution on the single thread?
options: Synchronous bytecode execution in separate threads
Event loop and non-blocking I/O callback queue
questions.explanation: JavaScript uses the event loop model with a call stack and callback/microtask queues to orchestrate asynchronous non-blocking tasks.

questions.question: Which SQL keyword is used to return only unique, non-repeating values in a query result set?
questions.explanation: The DISTINCT keyword in SQL eliminates duplicate records from the query result set.

questions.question: Which data structure follows the Last In, First Out (LIFO) order of execution?
questions.explanation: A Stack follows the Last In, First Out (LIFO) protocol where elements are pushed and popped from the top.

questions.question: In Object-Oriented Programming, when a child class provides a specific implementation of a method already defined in its superclass, this is known as:
questions.explanation: Method Overriding occurs when a subclass redefines a method from its superclass with the same signature.

questions.question: What is the average time complexity of searching for an element in a balanced Binary Search Tree (BST)?
questions.explanation: In a balanced BST with n nodes the height is about log2(n), yielding an average search complexity of O(log n).

questions.question: Which normal form requires removing transitive dependencies so that non-key attributes depend only on the primary key?
questions.explanation: Third Normal Form (3NF) mandates that a table is in 2NF and contains no transitive functional dependencies.

questions.question: In most programming languages that distinguish integer from floating-point arithmetic (such as C or Java), what is the value of the expression 7 / 2 when both operands are integers?
questions.explanation: Integer division discards (truncates) the fractional part, so 7 / 2 evaluates to 3.

questions.question: Which data type is designed to store a single logical value of either true or false?
questions.explanation: A boolean represents one of two truth values, true or false.

questions.question: In most programming languages, what does the boolean expression true && false evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Logical AND yields true only when both operands are true; here one operand is false, so the result is false.

questions.question: A variable that is declared inside a function and can only be accessed within that function is said to have which kind of scope?
questions.explanation: Variables declared inside a function are local to that function and are not visible outside it.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a symbol table in a compiler?
options: To track identifiers such as variables and functions along with their attributes
To store machine code instructions for the target CPU
To allocate physical memory for running programs
To schedule threads on the CPU
questions.explanation: A symbol table records identifiers and their properties, such as type, scope, and storage location, as the compiler analyzes the program.

questions.question: Which programming technique describes a function that calls itself as part of its own execution?
questions.explanation: Recursion is when a function invokes itself, typically with a base case that stops the chain of calls.

questions.question: What does it mean for a function argument to be passed by reference?
options: The function receives a copy of the argument's value
The argument is always converted to a string before being passed
The function receives access to the caller's original variable, so changes affect the caller
The function can only read the argument and can never modify it
questions.explanation: Passing by reference gives the function access to the original variable, so modifications made inside the function are visible to the caller.

questions.question: In a language that uses short-circuit evaluation, what is the result of evaluating the expression false && (1 / 0 == 0)?
options: It evaluates to false because the right operand is never evaluated
questions.explanation: With short-circuit AND, once the left operand is false the result is false and the right operand is not evaluated, avoiding the division by zero.

questions.question: Which data structure processes elements in First In, First Out (FIFO) order?
questions.explanation: A queue inserts at the rear and removes from the front, giving First In, First Out behavior.

questions.question: In a singly linked list, which operation can be performed in O(1) time when you already hold a pointer to a node?
options: Inserting a new node immediately after the given node
Searching for a value by key
Accessing the k-th element by index
questions.explanation: Inserting after a known node only requires a few pointer updates, whereas searching and indexing require traversal.

questions.question: Which data structure most directly models the call stack used to track function invocations in most programming languages?
questions.explanation: Function calls follow Last In, First Out semantics: the most recently called function must return before its caller resumes, which is a stack.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a min-heap from a binary search tree (BST)?
options: A min-heap is always perfectly balanced, while a BST never is
A min-heap supports O(log n) search for an arbitrary value just like a BST
A min-heap keeps each parent less than or equal to its children but does not order left versus right, while a BST orders all left descendants before the node and all right descendants after it
A min-heap stores elements in sorted order when its backing array is traversed front to back
questions.explanation: A heap only guarantees the parent-child ordering (the heap property); it does not maintain a global left/right ordering, so arbitrary search is not O(log n).

questions.question: What is the average-case time complexity of looking up a key in a well-implemented hash table?
questions.explanation: With a good hash function and a low load factor, keys spread evenly and lookups take constant expected time.

questions.question: In an AVL tree, what is the maximum allowed difference between the heights of the left and right subtrees of any node?
questions.explanation: The AVL balance condition requires the balance factor of every node to be -1, 0, or +1, meaning subtree heights differ by at most 1.

questions.question: Which traversal of a binary search tree visits its nodes in ascending key order?
questions.explanation: An in-order traversal (left, node, right) of a BST visits keys in sorted ascending order.

questions.question: Which algorithm is commonly used to find the shortest path from one source vertex to all other vertices in a graph with non-negative edge weights?
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm greedily expands the nearest unvisited vertex and works correctly when edge weights are non-negative.

questions.question: What precondition must an array satisfy before binary search can be applied?
options: It must contain only unique elements
It must have an even number of elements
It must be stored as a linked list
questions.explanation: Binary search repeatedly halves the search range by comparing the target with the middle element, which is only valid if the data is sorted.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n elements?
questions.explanation: The search interval halves with each comparison, giving about log2(n) steps.

questions.question: Which algorithmic paradigm does merge sort use?
questions.explanation: Merge sort divides the array into halves, sorts them recursively, and merges the sorted halves.

questions.question: Which algorithm computes a minimum spanning tree of a connected, weighted, undirected graph?
questions.explanation: Kruskal's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge that does not create a cycle.

questions.question: What does the Floyd-Warshall algorithm compute?
options: The single shortest path in a graph that may contain negative cycles
The maximum flow through a network
The shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in a weighted graph
A topological ordering of a directed acyclic graph
questions.explanation: Floyd-Warshall uses dynamic programming over intermediate vertices to compute all-pairs shortest paths in O(V^3) time.

questions.question: Which of the following decision problems is NP-complete?
options: Finding the shortest path between two nodes
Computing the greatest common divisor of two integers
questions.explanation: The Cook-Levin theorem establishes that SAT is NP-complete; the other listed problems are solvable in polynomial time.

questions.question: In SQL, which clause is used to filter individual rows before any grouping takes place?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows as they are read, whereas HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

questions.question: Which SQL statement is used to retrieve data from one or more tables?
questions.explanation: SELECT queries rows and columns from tables; the other statements modify stored data.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a JOIN in SQL?
options: To remove duplicate rows from a result
To combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column
questions.explanation: A JOIN links rows across tables using a matching condition, typically a primary-key to foreign-key relationship.

questions.question: Which type of join returns all rows from the left table and the matching rows from the right table, filling unmatched right-side columns with NULL?
questions.explanation: A LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves every row of the left table, filling unmatched right-side columns with NULL.

questions.question: Why can adding too many indexes to a database table reduce write performance?
options: Every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE must also update each affected index
Indexes compress the table's data and lose rows
Indexes prevent the use of transactions
Indexes force the table to be stored in memory only
questions.explanation: Indexes speed up reads but must be maintained on every write, so each additional index adds overhead to insert, update, and delete operations.

questions.question: What is the main responsibility of an operating system's CPU scheduler?
options: Translating virtual addresses to physical addresses
Managing the file system's directory structure
Deciding which ready process or thread runs on the CPU next
questions.explanation: The scheduler selects among ready tasks to allocate CPU time according to a scheduling policy.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of virtual memory?
options: To increase the clock speed of the CPU
To let all programs run without any memory protection
To let programs use an address space larger than the available physical memory
To eliminate the need for a file system
questions.explanation: Virtual memory maps program addresses to physical frames and can page data to disk, allowing programs to exceed physical RAM.

questions.question: What is thrashing in an operating system?
options: When two processes permanently block each other
When the CPU spends most of its time servicing page faults instead of executing useful work
When a process runs to completion without interruption
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when excessive paging keeps the system busy swapping pages, driving CPU utilization down.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock?
questions.explanation: The four Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait; 'preemption' is the opposite of the no-preemption condition.

questions.question: In a paged memory system, what does the page table map?
options: Virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers
questions.explanation: The page table translates each virtual page to the physical frame that currently holds it.

questions.question: What is the key advantage of a multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ) scheduler?
options: It guarantees every process a fixed, unchanging priority
It learns from a process's observed behavior and moves it between priority queues accordingly
It eliminates the need for context switching
It only schedules real-time tasks with hard deadlines
questions.explanation: MLFQ uses feedback such as CPU usage and I/O behavior to demote CPU-bound jobs and reward interactive ones by moving processes between queues.

questions.question: What does journaling provide in a file system?
options: Crash consistency by logging changes before writing them to their final locations
questions.explanation: A journal records intended updates first, so after a crash the file system can replay or discard incomplete transactions and remain consistent.

questions.question: In computer networking, what does the abbreviation IP stand for?
questions.explanation: IP is the Internet Protocol, responsible for addressing and routing packets across networks.

questions.question: Which transport-layer protocol is connection-oriented and provides reliable, ordered delivery?
questions.explanation: TCP establishes a connection, acknowledges data, and retransmits lost segments, providing reliable ordered delivery, whereas UDP is connectionless.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the Domain Name System (DNS)?
options: To translate human-readable domain names into IP addresses
To assign MAC addresses to network cards
To route packets between autonomous systems
questions.explanation: DNS resolves names such as example.com to the numeric IP addresses used by network devices.

questions.question: Which TCP port is used by HTTPS by default?
questions.explanation: HTTPS uses port 443 by default, while plain HTTP uses port 80.

questions.question: At which OSI model layer does a router primarily operate?
questions.explanation: Routers forward packets based on IP addresses, which is the network layer (Layer 3).

questions.question: What is the purpose of the TCP three-way handshake?
options: To establish a connection by synchronizing sequence numbers with SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK
To resolve domain names to IP addresses
To detect the maximum transmission unit (MTU) of the link
questions.explanation: The handshake exchanges SYN and ACK segments so both sides agree on initial sequence numbers before data transfer begins.

questions.question: What does a subnet mask define for an IPv4 address?
options: Which portion of the address identifies the network and which identifies the host
The maximum transmission unit of the link
The encryption algorithm used on the subnet
The physical MAC address of the gateway
questions.explanation: A subnet mask is a 32-bit value whose 1-bits mark the network prefix and 0-bits mark the host portion of an IPv4 address.

questions.question: What does encapsulation mean in object-oriented programming?
options: Allowing one interface to represent many implementations
Deriving new classes from existing ones
Splitting a program into multiple files
Bundling data with the methods that operate on it and restricting direct outside access
questions.explanation: Encapsulation hides internal state behind a public interface, typically using private fields and accessor methods.

questions.question: Which object-oriented principle allows different types to respond to the same method call in their own way?
questions.explanation: Polymorphism lets a single interface or method name behave differently depending on the actual object type, for example through overriding.

questions.question: What does inheritance allow in object-oriented programming?
options: A variable to hold several unrelated types at once
A class to acquire the fields and methods of a parent class
A program to run on multiple operating systems
questions.explanation: Inheritance creates an is-a relationship in which a subclass reuses and extends the behavior of a superclass.

questions.question: What is method overloading?
options: Defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class
Redefining a superclass method with an identical signature in a subclass
Hiding a field by giving it the same name as a local variable
Calling a method before it is defined
questions.explanation: Overloading distinguishes methods by their parameter signatures at compile time, whereas overriding replaces an inherited method with the same signature.

questions.question: What is a class that cannot be instantiated directly and is designed to be subclassed called?
questions.explanation: An abstract class may declare abstract methods and cannot be instantiated on its own; concrete subclasses must implement its abstract members.

questions.question: What does the Liskov Substitution Principle state?
options: A class should have only one reason to change
High-level modules should depend directly on low-level modules
Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without breaking the correctness of the program
An interface should be split into smaller, more specific interfaces
questions.explanation: LSP requires subtypes to preserve the behavior promised by their supertype so that client code can use them interchangeably.

questions.question: In the software development life cycle, what is the main deliverable of the requirements phase?
options: A specification describing what the system should do
questions.explanation: The requirements phase produces a documented description of the desired functionality and constraints before design and coding begin.

questions.question: In software engineering, what does the acronym DRY stand for?
questions.explanation: DRY advises against duplicating knowledge or logic, so each piece of behavior has a single authoritative representation.

questions.question: What is unit testing?
options: Testing individual functions or components in isolation
Testing the entire system with real users
Measuring the speed of the network
Reviewing code by reading it without executing it
questions.explanation: Unit tests exercise small, isolated pieces of code to verify their behavior independently of the rest of the system.

questions.question: In Agile software development, what is a sprint?
options: A permanent phase that never ends
A tool for compiling source code
A fixed, short time-boxed iteration of development work
questions.explanation: A sprint is a short, time-boxed period, often two to four weeks, during which a team completes a set of planned work.

questions.question: What is the primary goal of refactoring?
options: To reduce the number of developers needed
To improve the internal structure of code without changing its external behavior
To rewrite the application in a different language
questions.explanation: Refactoring restructures existing code to make it cleaner and more maintainable while preserving its observable behavior.

questions.question: What does Continuous Integration (CI) primarily involve?
options: Deploying every change straight to production without tests
Frequently merging developers' changes and automatically building and testing the integrated code
Writing documentation before writing any code
Freezing the codebase for long periods
questions.explanation: CI automates building and testing whenever changes are integrated, catching integration problems early.

questions.question: What does HTML stand for?
questions.explanation: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard language for structuring content on web pages.

questions.question: Which language is primarily used to style the appearance of web pages?
questions.explanation: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls the layout, colors, and typography of HTML documents.

questions.question: What does the HTTP status code 404 indicate?
options: The server encountered an internal error
The requested resource was not found
questions.explanation: 404 Not Found means the server could not locate the requested resource.

questions.question: In web development, what does REST describe?
options: An architectural style for web APIs that uses HTTP methods and stateless communication
questions.explanation: Representational State Transfer (REST) organizes APIs around resources addressed by URLs and manipulated with standard HTTP methods.

questions.question: What is an HTTP cookie primarily used for?
options: Storing small pieces of client-side data so the server can maintain state across requests
questions.explanation: Because HTTP is stateless, cookies let servers recognize clients across multiple requests, for example to keep a user logged in.

questions.question: According to the HTTP specification, which of these request methods is idempotent?
questions.explanation: PUT, like DELETE and the safe methods, is idempotent: repeating an identical request has the same intended effect as a single one, whereas POST is not.

questions.question: What does the security principle of least privilege mean?
options: All users should share one administrator account
Users and processes should be granted only the minimum access needed to perform their tasks
Passwords should be stored in plain text
Encryption should be disabled for speed
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits the access rights of users and programs to reduce the potential damage from errors or compromise.

questions.question: What is encryption?
options: Compressing data to save disk space
Encoding data so that only authorized parties can read it
Backing data up to a remote server
questions.explanation: Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext using a key so that only holders of the correct key can recover the original data.

questions.question: Which attack inserts malicious SQL statements through unsanitized user input?
questions.explanation: SQL injection occurs when untrusted input is concatenated into a query, allowing an attacker to alter its logic; parameterized queries prevent it.

questions.question: Why is a unique random salt added before hashing a password?
options: So identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed rainbow tables cannot be reused
To make the stored password shorter
To allow the password to be reversed later
questions.explanation: A per-password salt makes precomputed hash tables impractical and hides the fact that two users chose the same password.

questions.question: In HTTPS/TLS, what is the role of a Certificate Authority (CA)?
options: It encrypts all traffic between the client and server
It signs digital certificates vouching for the binding between a public key and an identity
It stores the server's private key
It assigns IP addresses to servers
questions.explanation: A trusted CA digitally signs a server's certificate, letting clients verify that the public key belongs to the claimed identity.

questions.question: What is a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack?
options: An attacker floods a server with traffic until it becomes unavailable
An attacker guesses passwords by trying common dictionary words
An attacker secretly relays and possibly alters communication between two parties who believe they are talking directly to each other
An attacker reads data from a discarded hard drive
questions.explanation: In a MITM attack the adversary positions itself between two communicating parties and can eavesdrop on or modify their traffic.

questions.question: In computing, what does 'the cloud' generally refer to?
options: A physical server located in the user's office
On-demand computing resources delivered over the internet
questions.explanation: Cloud computing provides computing, storage, and services on demand over a network, typically with pay-as-you-go pricing.

questions.question: What is a container, such as one managed by Docker?
options: A lightweight, isolated package of an application together with its dependencies
questions.explanation: Containers package an application and its libraries so it runs consistently across environments while sharing the host operating system kernel.

questions.question: Adding more machines or instances to handle increased load is known as:
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds more instances, whereas vertical scaling (scaling up) increases the resources of a single machine.

questions.question: What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC)?
options: Writing application source code directly on a remote server
Documenting servers manually in a spreadsheet
Managing and provisioning infrastructure through machine-readable configuration files
questions.explanation: IaC defines servers, networks, and other resources declaratively in files that can be version-controlled and applied automatically.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of a blue-green deployment?
options: Doubling the number of servers permanently
Eliminating the need for automated tests
Reducing downtime and risk by switching traffic between two identical environments
Running two different versions of the database simultaneously forever
questions.explanation: Two identical environments let a team release to the idle one, verify it, and then switch traffic with a fast rollback if problems appear.

questions.question: In Kubernetes, what is a Pod?
options: A single physical server in the cluster
The smallest deployable unit, containing one or more containers that share network and storage resources
questions.explanation: A Pod is Kubernetes' atomic scheduling unit; its containers are co-located and share the same network namespace and volumes.

questions.question: What kind of tool is Git?
questions.explanation: Git is a distributed version control system: every clone contains the full history, and changes can be committed locally and shared later.

questions.question: Which Git command creates a new branch and immediately switches to it?
questions.explanation: git checkout -b <name> creates the branch and checks it out in one step; git switch -c is the modern equivalent.

questions.question: When run on the main branch, what does the command git merge feature do?
options: It deletes the feature branch permanently
It creates a new remote repository
It integrates the changes from the feature branch into the current branch
It reverts all commits on the feature branch
questions.explanation: git merge combines the history of another branch into the currently checked-out branch, possibly creating a merge commit.

questions.question: In Git, what is a commit?
options: A request to the remote server for permissions
A temporary file that is never saved
A list of files that are ignored
A snapshot of the staged changes, together with a message and metadata
questions.explanation: A commit records the state of the staged files at a point in time and links to its parent commit, forming the project history.

questions.question: What does git rebase do?
options: It reapplies commits from one branch onto another, rewriting them to create a linear history
It downloads the entire repository again
It creates a copy of the remote branch locally
questions.explanation: Rebase moves or replays a series of commits onto a new base, producing a linear history but changing the affected commit hashes.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of accessing an array element by its index?
questions.explanation: Because array elements are stored contiguously, the address of the i-th element is computed directly, giving constant-time access.

questions.question: In Big-O notation, what does O(n) describe?
options: An algorithm with constant running time
An algorithm that runs in logarithmic time
An algorithm whose running time grows linearly with the input size
questions.explanation: O(n) means the time or space grows proportionally to the size of the input.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of the best possible comparison-based sorting algorithm?
questions.explanation: Any comparison-based sort requires at least about n log n comparisons in the worst case, and algorithms such as merge sort and heap sort achieve O(n log n).

questions.question: What is the auxiliary space complexity of the standard merge sort algorithm on an array of n elements?
questions.explanation: Standard merge sort allocates temporary arrays while merging, requiring O(n) additional space; the recursion stack adds only O(log n).

questions.question: What is the amortized time complexity of appending an element to a dynamic array (such as an ArrayList or Python list) that doubles its capacity when full?
questions.explanation: Occasional resizes cost O(n), but they are rare enough that the cost averaged over many appends is constant, i.e. amortized O(1).

questions.question: What is the main job of a compiler?
options: To execute a program line by line
To translate source code into machine code or another target language
questions.explanation: A compiler translates a program written in a source language into an equivalent program in a target language, such as machine code.

questions.question: Which phase of compilation converts a stream of source characters into tokens?
questions.explanation: The lexer (scanner) groups characters into tokens such as identifiers, keywords, and operators.

questions.question: What best describes an interpreter?
options: It converts source code into a standalone binary before running it
It executes a program directly, typically statement by statement, without producing a separate executable
It links object files into an executable
It stores the program's variables in a database
questions.explanation: An interpreter reads and executes source or bytecode directly at run time, rather than compiling the whole program to machine code ahead of time.

questions.question: What is the parser's role in a compiler?
options: To build a syntax structure such as a parse tree from the token stream according to the grammar
To assign physical registers to variables
To remove comments from the source file
To link libraries into the final program
questions.explanation: The parser checks that the token sequence conforms to the language grammar and produces a structured representation for later phases.

questions.question: Why do many compilers translate source code into an intermediate representation (IR) before generating machine code?
options: Because the IR is the final executable format
Because IR replaces the need for a parser
Because IR lets programs run without a CPU
Because an IR is machine-independent, enabling shared optimization and easier retargeting to different CPUs
questions.explanation: A machine-independent IR lets the compiler run optimizations once and then generate code for multiple target architectures.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a load balancer in system design?
options: To store the contents of a database
To distribute incoming requests across multiple servers
questions.explanation: A load balancer spreads traffic over a pool of servers to improve availability and handle more concurrent requests.

questions.question: Why is a database replica commonly maintained?
options: To replace the need for backups entirely
To serve read traffic and provide a standby for failover
To increase the write capacity of the primary
To store the application's source code
questions.explanation: Replicas copy data from a primary so read load can be shared and a standby is available if the primary fails.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a cache in a system?
options: To store frequently accessed data close to the consumer to reduce latency and load on slower storage
To permanently archive all user data
To increase the size of the primary database
questions.explanation: Caches keep hot data in fast storage such as memory or a nearby service so repeated reads avoid slower backends.

questions.question: What does the CAP theorem state about a distributed data system?
options: It must always be both consistent and available
It must process every request in constant time
It guarantees all three properties if enough servers are added
It can guarantee at most two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance simultaneously
questions.explanation: The CAP theorem proves that a networked data system cannot simultaneously guarantee consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.
